title: Centralizers of tori in smooth connected affine groups are smooth and connected
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroup schemes are closed [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness is as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and connectedness as in [def-weil-connected-scheme]; geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure $\bar k$. A torus is a group scheme $T$ with $T_{\bar k}\simeq(\mathbf G_m)^r$ for some integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. For a subgroup $H\subseteq G$, its centralizer functor is $C_G(H)(A)=\{g\in G(A):g_{A\prime}h=hg_{A\prime}\text{ for every commutative }A\text{-algebra }A\prime\text{ and every }h\in H(A\prime)\}$. Let $G$ be smooth and geometrically connected and let $T\subseteq G$ be any torus. Then $C_G(T)$ is represented by a smooth geometrically connected closed subgroup scheme of $G$. No reductivity or maximality is assumed.

source.place: Corollary 13.10, printed p.257 (smoothness); Theorem 17.38, printed p.363 (connectedness), applied after extension to an algebraic closure; Proposition 1.92 and following paragraph, printed pp.33--34 (centralizer functor).

proof.text: Write $G=\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $T=\operatorname{Spec}D$. By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], $G\times_kG=\operatorname{Spec}(R\otimes_kR)$. Its coordinate algebra is generated by the two copies of any finite generating set of $R$, so it is of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. The diagonal is induced by the surjection $R\otimes_kR\to R$, $u\otimes v\mapsto uv$, hence is closed [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Thus $G$ is separated [def-weil-proper-morphism]. The same diagonal calculation for $D$ and $R\otimes_kR$ shows that $T$ and $G\times_kG$ are separated as well. These verify all the scheme hypotheses for the factorization locus used next.

source.place: Proposition 1.92, printed p.33: separatedness and closed diagonal, checked on coordinate algebras.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] with $Y=T$, parameter scheme $S=G$, target $X=G\times_kG$, $W=\Delta_G(G)$ and $f(t,g)=(t,gtg^{-1})$, where $t$ in the target is its image under $T\hookrightarrow G$. This is a morphism by [def-sc-group-scheme]. We obtain a closed subscheme $C\hookrightarrow G$ representing exactly those $g:Z\to G$ for which conjugation by $g$ on $T\times_kZ$ agrees with the inclusion into $G\times_kZ$. For $Z=\operatorname{Spec}A$, this equality implies the commuting identity after every extension $A\to A\prime$. Conversely, apply the identities in the statement to $A\prime=A\otimes_kD$ and the universal point of $T_A$. Equality there says the two coordinate maps agree [def-weil-affine-spectrum], hence says exactly that $f$ factors through the diagonal. Thus $C$ represents the stated centralizer functor, not merely its field-valued points.

source.place: Proposition 1.92, printed p.33; Theorem 1.105, printed pp.37–38, universal factorization locus; explicit universal-point verification.

proof.text: For every $A$, the identity belongs to $C(A)$. If $g,h\in C(A)$ and $t\in T(A\prime)$, then $(gh)t=g(th)=t(gh)$ and $g^{-1}t=tg^{-1}$ in $G(A\prime)$. Thus $C(A)$ is a subgroup, naturally in $A$, so $C$ is a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Since $C\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}R$ is closed, $C=\operatorname{Spec}(R/I)$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]; the images of generators of $R$ generate $R/I$, so $C$ is affine of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. The same construction works for every smooth affine finite-type group and torus, without using connectedness.

source.place: Proposition 1.92, printed pp.33–34: the represented subfunctor is a subgroup; coordinate quotient gives finite type.

proof.text: Let $T$ act on the smooth affine scheme $G$ by $a(t,g)=tgt^{-1}$. The group laws give an action. On every $A$ and every $A\prime/A$, $a(t,g_{A\prime})=g_{A\prime}$ is equivalent to $tg_{A\prime}=g_{A\prime}t$. Hence the fixed subfunctor is exactly the functor represented by $C$ in step 2. Apply [lem-sfb-torus-fixed-scheme-smooth] with $X=G$ and $F=C$. The assumed smoothness of $G$, its affine finite type, the torus hypothesis on $T$, and the closed representability of $C$ verify every hypothesis. It follows that $C$ is smooth over $k$.

source.place: Theorem 13.1, printed p.254, specialized as in the proof of Corollary 13.10, printed p.257.

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $K=\bar k$. The scheme $G_K$ is smooth by [lem-pc-proper-base-change](2), and connected by the assumed geometric connectedness. Tensoring the finite generating sets shows $G_K$ and $T_K$ are affine of finite type, and $T_K\simeq(\mathbf G_m)^r$. The fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product] identifies $C_K(A)$ with $C(A)$ for any $K$-algebra $A$. Every $k$-algebra extension of $A$ acquires its unique compatible $K$-algebra structure from $K\to A$, and conversely every $K$-algebra extension is such a $k$-algebra extension. The defining commuting tests are therefore identical. Consequently $C_K$ represents $C_{G_K}(T_K)$. It remains to prove connectedness over this algebraically closed field.

source.place: Paragraph after Proposition 1.92, printed p.34, field base change; Theorem 17.38, printed p.363, reduction to an algebraic closure.

proof.text: Fix any $c\in C_K(K)$. By [lem-sfb-torus-commuting-point-common-borel], there is a Borel subgroup $B\subseteq G_K$ containing $T_K$ and $c$. In particular $B$ is smooth, connected, solvable, affine and of finite type. Apply [lem-sfb-torus-regular-semisimple-element] to $T_K\subseteq B$. It gives a semisimple $s\in T_K(K)$ whose centralizer functor in $B$ is exactly that of $T_K$, on all algebras. The semisimple centralizer is connected by [lem-sfb-solvable-semisimple-centralizer-connected], applied to $B$ and $s$. Thus the subgroup scheme $D=C_B(T_K)=C_B(s)$ is connected. The equality is equality of represented subfunctors, not just equality of rational points. Its inclusion into $G_K$ factors through $C_K$ by the commuting tests of step 2. It contains both the identity and $c$. This constructs a connected subspace of $C_K$ through the identity and each of its rational points.

source.place: Theorem 17.38, printed p.363, using Lemma 17.37; Theorems 16.40–16.41 and Lemma 16.42, printed pp.338–339. The reduction from torus to semisimple centralizers is made explicit.

proof.text: Suppose $C_K=U\amalg V$ is a disjoint clopen decomposition, and label its parts so that the identity lies in $U$ [def-weil-connected-scheme]. For every $c\in C_K(K)$, the connected $D$ of step 6 has a disjoint clopen decomposition by its inverse images of $U,V$. Its identity lies in the first part, so the second is empty. In particular $c\in U$, and $V$ contains no $K$-point. By [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], closed points of the affine finite-type scheme $C_K$ lying in $V$ are dense in $V$. By clause (1) of [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing], each such closed point is a $K$-point. There are none, so density forces $V=\varnothing$. Thus $C_K$ is connected. This argument needs no finite family of Borels and no equality between an infinite scheme-theoretic union and a pointwise union. Since $C$ is smooth by step 4 and $C_{\bar k}$ is connected, it has all the properties asserted in the item.

source.place: Theorem 17.38, printed p.363, union through the identity rewritten as a clopen-separation argument; Stacks 0478, varieties lemma-locally-finite-type-Jacobson, for density.

proof_origin.place: Proposition 1.92 and following paragraph, pp.33–34; Theorem 13.1 and Corollary 13.10, pp.254–257; Theorems 16.40–16.41, Lemma 16.42, pp.338–339; Lemma 17.37 and Theorem 17.38, p.363. The last union argument is written as a clopen test, correcting the unnecessary finite-union parenthesis.
